summary: This program builds a shelter that holds robot pet objects in a private list — an example of composition, where one object is made up of others. The shelter can add pets, print a report on all of them, and look one up by name.

lines.text: The shelter is not a kind of robot pet, so it does not inherit from anything; it simply contains pets. That relationship is called composition.
The two leading underscores make the list private, so outside code cannot reach in and modify the shelter's pets directly. Everything must go through the methods below.
This is the only doorway into the private list, which lets the class control how pets get added.
An empty list is falsy in Python, so this reads as "if there are no pets yet" and avoids printing a blank report.
Joining with a newline character turns the collection of pet descriptions into one multi-line string that the caller can print in a single step.
`type(pet).__name__` asks each object what class it came from, so the report shows RobotCat, RobotBird, or RobotDog without the shelter having to keep track.
This generator expression produces one formatted line per pet, feeding them into the join above.
A search method lets callers retrieve a pet object by name instead of needing access to the private list.
Lowercasing both sides makes the search case-insensitive, so "rex" and "Rex" both find the same dog.
When the loop finishes without a match, returning None gives the caller a clear "not found" answer to test for.
Each pet is created independently of the shelter; the shelter will hold references to these existing objects.
A fresh shelter starts with an empty private list of pets.
Handing the cat to the shelter stores it inside the private list, and the shelter can now include it in reports and searches.
One call produces the whole report, because the shelter loops over its pets for you.
The search returns the actual RobotDog object, not just its name, so its methods can be called next.
Guarding on the result avoids an error if the search returned None because no pet matched.
Because the returned object is a real RobotDog, calling show_talent() runs the dog's own version of that method.
